582.title: The Lord turned and looked (Luke 22:54–71)
582.hook: at the third denial, Jesus turns and looks at Peter
582.howItsDone: Christians read Peter's denial during Holy Week, and tradition links the rooster on some church steeples to Peter's denial and his return.

segments.voice: Yesterday, he touched his ear and healed the man who came to arrest him. Your line was no more of this. What did you start to mend? Day five hundred eighty-two.

They take Jesus to the high priest's house. Peter follows, Luke says, afar off. Close enough to see. Far enough to leave. In the middle of the courtyard someone has kindled a fire, and people are sitting around it, and Peter sits down with them. Warm hands, firelight on faces. A servant girl looks at him for a long moment and says, this man was with him too. Peter says, woman, I don't know him. A little later someone else: you're one of them. Man, I'm not. About an hour passes. Then a third person is certain: he's a Galilean, he was with him. Matthew adds that his accent gives him away.

Peter answers the third time: man, I don't know what you're saying. And while he's still speaking, the rooster crows. Then comes the line that only Luke has, in the King James words: "And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And Peter went out, and wept bitterly." Luke doesn't say exactly where Jesus is, only that he's close enough to turn and see Peter. Earlier that night, at the table, Jesus told Peter, I have prayed for you, that your faith fail not. Now, across a courtyard, one look. Luke doesn't describe it. He doesn't say angry or sad or kind. He just says the Lord turned and looked. And the look sends Peter out into the night, weeping. Preachers and painters have imagined that look ever since. Some hear it as the opposite of a glare: the look of someone who already knew, already prayed, and still hasn't let go of him. Notice too that Peter's tears are the beginning, not the end, of his story. After that, Luke goes on: the men holding Jesus mock him, blindfold him, hit him, and say, prophesy, who struck you? At daybreak the council asks him, are you the Christ? And he answers that if he told them, they wouldn't believe him. The night is long. But Luke wants you to remember one moment from it: a man who just failed three times, and the face he saw when he looked up.
screen: `TEARS ARE NOT THE END FOR PETER.`
then, large: `THE LORD TURNED, AND LOOKED UPON PETER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: imagine a look of love, not blame. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you did that you're ashamed of. Not the worst thing, just something that still stings. Now imagine someone who loves you finding out, and turning to look at you. It's easy to imagine a glare. Try instead a face that already knew, and isn't leaving. Stay with that face for a minute. If you pray, you can imagine it as the face of Christ. The bell holds the time.
The Lord turned and looked. Luke's single line at the third denial: no words, only a look across the courtyard, and Peter remembers and weeps.
screen: `THE LORD TURNED AND LOOKED — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the lord looked at peter. Today, when someone lets you down, try to look at them the way you'd hope to be looked at. Day five hundred eighty-two.

583.title: Herod's laughter (Luke 23:1–12)
583.hook: sent to Herod, he says nothing, and two enemies become friends that day
583.howItsDone: Churches that follow a three-year cycle of readings hear Luke's account of the trial, Herod's scene included, on Palm Sunday in the year of Luke; some readers connect Jesus's silence with the servant of Isaiah 53.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rooster, a fire, and the Lord turned and looked. Your line was the lord looked at peter. Who did you try to look at with kindness instead of blame? Day five hundred eighty-three.

Morning. The council brings Jesus to Pilate, the Roman governor, with charges that would worry any Roman: he stirs up the nation, forbids paying taxes to Caesar, calls himself a king. Luke's readers have already heard him on taxes: render to Caesar what is Caesar's. Pilate asks one question and announces: "I find no fault in this man." But they keep pressing. He started in Galilee, they say. Galilee. Pilate hears a way out. Galilee belongs to Herod, and Herod happens to be in Jerusalem at the time. Send the problem across town.
screen: `I FIND NO FAULT IN THIS MAN.`

segments.voice: This is Herod the tetrarch, ruler of Galilee. Earlier in Luke he's the man who says he beheaded John the Baptist, and Jesus once called him that fox. Herod is thrilled. Luke says he'd wanted to see Jesus for a long time, and hoped to see him do a miracle. Herod fires questions, many words, the King James says. And then: "he answered him nothing." Nothing. Jesus has talked his whole way through this Gospel, to crowds, to sinners, to Pharisees at dinner, and soon to a thief on a cross. Before this man he goes silent. Some readers hear an echo of Isaiah's servant, brought as a lamb to the slaughter, who opened not his mouth. The chief priests and scribes stand by, accusing him hard. So Herod and his soldiers turn to mockery. They treat him with contempt, laugh at him, dress him in a gorgeous robe like a costume king, and send him back to Pilate. Then Luke adds a strange, bitter line found in no other Gospel: "And the same day Pilate and Herod were made friends together: for before they were at enmity between themselves." Two rulers who couldn't stand each other find common ground in a joke at the expense of a silent man. Luke doesn't explain the silence. Some readers hear dignity: some questions don't deserve an answer. Others hear refusal: he will not perform for a ruler who only wants a show. Either way, the miracle Herod hoped for never comes.

Here's the practice: stay silent before mockery. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place where you get baited: a comment section, a relative who likes to poke, a coworker's jokes. Picture the moment the jab lands. Notice the heat that rises, the reply forming in your mouth. Now imagine just letting the moment pass. Not sulking, not plotting. Simply not performing. Breathe through it. If you pray, you can ask God for that kind of quiet. The bell holds the time.
Herod's laughter. The ruler who wanted a miracle got silence, and answered it with mockery and a borrowed robe.
Your line: he answered nothing. Today, when someone baits you for a show, let one jab go by without answering it. Day five hundred eighty-three.

584.title: Release Barabbas (Luke 23:13–25)
584.hook: Pilate says three times he finds no fault, and yields to the shouts
584.howItsDone: In some churches the Passion is read aloud on Palm Sunday and Good Friday with the congregation speaking the crowd's lines, so that the shout belongs to everyone in the room rather than to someone else.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herod's laughter, and a man who would not perform. Your line was he answered nothing. Which jab did you let go by? Day five hundred eighty-four.

Pilate has already said it once: I find no fault in this man. Then he sent Jesus to Herod, and Herod sent him back, still in the gorgeous robe. So it's Pilate's problem again. He calls together the chief priests, the rulers and the people, and gives the Roman governor's verdict. A verdict is supposed to settle things. Someone in charge knows the right answer and says it out loud. What happens next is a story about what that answer is worth when the room gets loud, and keeps getting louder.

Pilate says it plainly: I've examined him, and I find no fault in him. Neither did Herod. I'll have him beaten, and let him go. And the crowd in front of him cries out, all together, away with this man, release unto us Barabbas. Luke tells us who Barabbas is: a man thrown in prison for an uprising in the city, and for murder. Pilate speaks to them again, wanting to release Jesus. They shout, crucify him. Then, in the King James words: "And he said unto them the third time, Why, what evil hath he done? I have found no cause of death in him: I will therefore chastise him, and let him go." Three times, no fault. Luke counts them so you'll notice. "And they were instant with loud voices, requiring that he might be crucified. And the voices of them and of the chief priests prevailed." The voices prevailed. Not the evidence. Not the law. The volume. Pilate releases the man jailed for murder, and hands Jesus over to their will. Two things are worth holding carefully here. First, this is one crowd before Pilate on one morning, with its leaders, not a whole people. Christians in the past used scenes like this to blame the Jewish people for Jesus's death, with terrible results, and churches, the Catholic Church among them, have since formally rejected that reading. The sentence was Rome's, and the cross was a Roman punishment. Second, the man with the power knew the truth, said it three times, and gave it up.
screen: then, large: `I HAVE FOUND NO CAUSE OF DEATH IN HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: don't yield to one loud crowd. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you know is right, or true, that you've gone quiet about because people around you are loud. At work, in your family, online, in your own head. Say it to yourself plainly, once. Then a second time. Then a third. Notice whether it still feels true. You don't have to fight anyone today. Just don't hand it over. If you pray, you can ask God for steadiness. The bell holds the time.
Release Barabbas. The crowd's cry before Pilate: free the man jailed for uprising and murder, and crucify the one the governor found innocent.
Your line: three times, no fault. Today, when the room gets loud, say the true thing you know one more time, calmly, before you let it go. Day five hundred eighty-four.

585.title: Daughters of Jerusalem (Luke 23:26–31)
585.hook: carrying the cross, he stops to comfort weeping women
585.howItsDone: Many Christians, especially Catholics and Anglicans, pray the Stations of the Cross on the Fridays of Lent, stopping at the eighth station to remember Jesus meeting the women of Jerusalem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, release Barabbas, and the voices that prevailed. Your line was three times, no fault. What true thing did you say once more when the room got loud? Day five hundred eighty-five.

A man is coming into the city from the countryside, minding his own business. His name is Simon, and he's from Cyrene, in North Africa. Suddenly soldiers grab him and put a wooden beam on his shoulders, and he's walking behind a condemned man he's never met. That's how Luke starts the road to the cross: with a stranger forced to help. Behind them follows a great crowd of people, and among them, women. They're beating their breasts and wailing, the way people mourned the dead. And then Jesus, who has barely spoken since the courtyard, stops and turns to them.
screen: `SIMON OF CYRENE, PULLED FROM THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children." Think about where he is. Beaten through the night, mocked by soldiers, now walking to his own execution. Every reason to be wrapped up in his own pain. And he turns to the people grieving for him and thinks about them. He looks ahead to days of suffering coming for that city, when people will call the childless blessed and ask the mountains to fall on them. Then a proverb, hard to translate and harder to pin down: "For if they do these things in a green tree, what shall be done in the dry?" Green wood is hard to burn; dry wood catches at once. One common reading goes like this: if this is what's done to an innocent man now, think how much worse it will be when the times are dry. Scholars debate who the they is and exactly what's meant; the saying is short and doesn't explain itself. Many connect his warning to the Roman siege of Jerusalem a generation later. Only Luke tells this scene: women openly mourning him on the road, and Jesus stopping to speak to them. Later it became part of the Stations of the Cross, the devotion where Christians walk the way to Calvary in fourteen stops. Jesus meeting the women of Jerusalem is the eighth. On the worst day of his life, he still turns toward someone else's grief.
screen: then, large: `DAUGHTERS OF JERUSALEM, WEEP NOT FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: comfort someone while you're struggling. Settle, and breathe. Name honestly what's hard for you right now. Let it be real. Then, without pushing it away, think of one person near you who is also carrying something. A friend after a breakup. A coworker with a sick parent. A neighbor who's lonely. Picture one small comfort you could offer them today, even from inside your own hard week. A text. A coffee. Ten minutes of listening. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Daughters of Jerusalem. The women who mourned Jesus on the road to the cross, and whom he stopped to speak to.
Your line: weep not for me. Today, even if your own week is hard, turn toward one person who's hurting and offer them something small. Day five hundred eighty-five.

586.title: Father, forgive them (Luke 23:32–43)
586.hook: he forgives his executioners and promises paradise to a dying thief
586.carry: they know not what they do
586.howItsDone: On Good Friday some churches hold services on the seven last words of Christ from the cross; the first two are Father, forgive them, and the promise of paradise to the penitent thief.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daughters of Jerusalem, and Jesus turning to comfort them. Your line was weep not for me. Who did you turn toward, even in a hard week? Day five hundred eighty-six.

A Persian king's garden. High walls around it, and inside, water running in channels, fruit trees, shade, quiet. Dictionaries trace the word paradise back to an old Persian word for an enclosure like that. It passed into Greek, and in the Greek translation of Genesis it names the garden God planted in Eden. Keep that walled garden in mind. Now set it beside the ugliest place in the story: the place the King James calls Calvary, and the Greek calls the Skull. Three crosses. Jesus in the middle, a criminal on each side. Today's word comes from the garden, and it is spoken there.

Luke gives us two sayings from the cross that no other Gospel has. The first comes as they crucify him, in the King James words: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." Then they divide his clothes by casting lots. He's praying for the people doing it, while they're doing it. A careful note: some early copies of Luke don't have this prayer, and others do. The second comes later. The crowd stares. The leaders sneer. The soldiers mock. One of the criminals hanging beside him joins in: aren't you the Christ? Save yourself and us. But the other one tells him to stop. We deserve this, he says. This man has done nothing wrong. Then he speaks to Jesus: "Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." Not save me. Just remember me. And Jesus answers: "Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." Paradise: Christians hear in it the garden restored, life with God. Promised to a man with no time left to earn anything. Christians read the promise in more than one way. Some hear it as rest with God right after death, before the final resurrection. Others place the comma after today, I tell you today, and read the promise as future; the old Greek copies had little punctuation, so the comma is a translator's choice. Either way, in Luke the last person Jesus speaks to from the cross, apart from his Father, is a criminal, and he says yes.
screen: then, large: `TO DAY SHALT THOU BE WITH ME IN PARADISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive someone who doesn't know better. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who hurt you without really understanding what they were doing. A parent doing their best with what they had. A kid who said something cruel. A stranger who cut you off. Hold them in your mind. Notice that they didn't see the whole picture. If you pray, you can say Jesus's words for them: Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do. If you don't, simply try loosening your grip on it, even a little. The bell holds the time.
Paradise. From an old Persian word for a walled garden, used in Greek for Eden; the place Jesus promises the dying thief, today.
Your line: they know not what they do. Today, when someone hurts you without seeing it, try saying this line in your head before you answer. Day five hundred eighty-six.

587.title: Into your hands (Luke 23:44–56)
587.hook: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit; the women prepare spices
587.tomorrow: why seek the living among the dead?
587.howItsDone: In Compline, the church's night prayer, the words 'into thy hands' are said or sung as the day ends, and on Good Friday the last words from the cross are read and remembered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, paradise, promised to a dying thief. Your line was they know not what they do. When did you say it before you answered someone? Day five hundred eighty-seven.

Some prayers are learned so early that they're there when nothing else is. A child's bedtime prayer. A line a grandmother said every night. At the end, the line Jesus reaches for comes from Psalm thirty-one. It's about the sixth hour, around noon, and Luke says darkness covers the whole land until the ninth hour, around three in the afternoon. The sun's light fails. In the temple, the curtain of the sanctuary is torn down the middle. And Jesus, who has been praying all through this Gospel, prays one last time, with a line from the prayers of his people.

In the King James words: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit: and having said thus, he gave up the ghost." Commend means to hand over, to entrust, the way you'd give someone you love into another's care. The psalm says it this way in the King James: "Into thine hand I commit my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O LORD God of truth." Jesus adds one word to the front of it: Father. In Mark and Matthew, the last words Jesus speaks from the cross come from a different psalm, my God, why hast thou forsaken me. Luke gives us this one instead. Christians keep both, and some hear in them two sides of the same death: the cry of abandonment, and the word of trust. Then Luke turns to the people watching. A Roman centurion glorifies God and says, "Certainly this was a righteous man." The crowds go home beating their breasts. His friends, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, stand at a distance and watch. Then a man named Joseph, from Arimathea, steps forward. He's a member of the council, and Luke tells us he hadn't agreed with their decision. He asks Pilate for the body, wraps it in linen, and lays it in a tomb cut into rock, where no one had ever been laid. The women follow and see where. They go home and prepare spices and ointments. And then, Luke says, they rested on the sabbath, according to the commandment. Even in grief, they keep the sabbath, and wait.
screen: then, large: `INTO THY HANDS I COMMEND MY SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the words before sleep. You can begin now. Settle, and breathe. Think of what you'll carry into bed tonight: your body, tired; your worries; the people you love. Imagine opening your hands and placing each one into hands larger than yours. You don't have to know how it will turn out. If you pray, you can say it, now and tonight before sleep: into thy hands I commend my spirit. If you don't, simply open your hands on your lap and let the day go. The bell holds the time.
Into your hands. Jesus's last words from the cross in Luke, from Psalm thirty-one: a psalm of trust, with Father added, spoken at the end.
Your line: into your hands. Tonight, before you sleep, open your hands, say the line, and name the people you're handing over. Day five hundred eighty-seven.

588.title: Why seek the living among the dead? (Luke 24:1–12)
588.word: Why seek the living among the dead?
588.hook: the women tell the apostles, who think it idle tales
588.tomorrow: known in the breaking of bread
588.howItsDone: Christians celebrate the resurrection every Easter and gather on Sundays because the tomb was found empty on the first day of the week; Orthodox Christians honor the women who came with spices as the Myrrh-bearers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, into your hands, the last words from the cross, and spices prepared for the tomb. Your line was into your hands. Did you open your hands before sleep? Day five hundred eighty-eight.

Sunday, very early. The sabbath is over. A small group of women set out in the gray light, carrying the spices they prepared before the sabbath. They are going to do the last thing love can do for a body. They know exactly where the tomb is; they watched Joseph lay him there. They are not expecting anything. And when they arrive, the stone is already rolled away from the entrance. They go inside. The body isn't there. Luke says they were much perplexed. And then, suddenly, two men are standing beside them in shining garments.

The women are terrified and bow their faces to the ground. And the two men ask a question, in the King James words: "Why seek ye the living among the dead? He is not here, but is risen." Then: remember what he told you in Galilee, that the Son of man must be delivered, crucified, and rise again the third day. Luke says, simply, they remembered his words. Notice who's being reminded. These women had been listening all along, back in Galilee. They're disciples. Luke even names them: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and other women with them. They go back and tell the eleven and the rest. And then this, in the King James words: "And their words seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not." Idle tales. The Greek word is lēros: nonsense, empty talk. So in Luke the news of the resurrection comes first from women, and the men dismiss it. Luke doesn't hide it. He tells it plainly, and some readers see that plainness as a mark of honesty. Then Peter gets up and runs to the tomb anyway. He stoops down, sees the linen cloths lying by themselves, and goes home wondering. Not sure yet. Wondering. The women were right first.
screen: then, large: `HE IS NOT HERE, BUT IS RISEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: believe a woman's testimony. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time, if there was one, when a woman said something true and wasn't taken seriously, by you or by the people around you. A mother who saw a problem coming. A colleague whose idea got credited to someone else. A friend who said something was wrong and was told she was overreacting. Hold that memory honestly. Then think of one woman whose word you could take more seriously this week, and how you'd show it. If you pray, you can give thanks for her. The bell holds the time.
Why seek the living among the dead? The question at the empty tomb, asked of the women who came with spices for a body that wasn't there.
screen: `WHY SEEK THE LIVING AMONG THE DEAD? — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: he is not here. This week went from Peter's tears to Herod, Barabbas, the road, the cross, the tomb, and this question. Today, when a woman tells you something, listen all the way through, and believe her first. Day five hundred eighty-eight, and another week on the path.

fork.setup: you're one of the eleven. some women burst in saying the tomb is empty and he is risen. what do you do?
options: believe them and run to tell others.
think it's nonsense and stay put.
go and see for yourself.
fork.reveal: their words seemed to them as idle tales. Peter got up and ran to the tomb anyway, and even he went home wondering.

original.note: Greek: nonsense, idle talk. Luke's word for how the women's report sounded to the apostles.

trapdoor: what you thought: the women found an empty tomb and everyone celebrated.
what it means: the women were reminded, remembered, and told; the men called it nonsense; and Peter went home wondering.
what a scholar hears: leros is a blunt word for nonsense; and some readers take an account that makes the apostles look slow as a mark of honesty.
